---
title: "Part 3 · What default hyperpriors imply"
description: "Nine published ways to choose the Gamma hyperprior on alpha, what each implies for the number of clusters and for their sizes, and where each goes wrong."
---

Every rule for choosing the Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on alpha answers one question and leaves
another open. Read through two lenses at once, the **count** (K_J, the number of fitted
components among the J units) and the **weights** (W_SB, the share of the cluster that a
randomly chosen unit belongs to), each published rule says something its users did not ask
for. Select a year for its one-line error, the evidence and a link to its explorer.

## The story in six steps

1. **The vague default.** Gamma(1, 1) is vague about alpha, not about clusters. The
   expected count drifts with the design (E K_J = 4.16 at J = 50, 6.44 at J = 500) while a
   random unit's chance of sitting in a majority-mass cluster stays at .591 for every J.
   The "conservative" defaults Gamma(1, 3) and Gamma(2, 4) raise that chance to .812 and
   .726. See [Same default, different J](defaults-drift.qmd) and
   [What Gamma(1, 1) actually says](../bridge/gamma11.qmd).
2. **DORO** (Dorazio, 2009) projects onto a flat count target. A Gamma mixture cannot be
   flat: the closest one is a spike at one cluster plus a hump near n, the gap grows with n,
   and the prior ends up expecting about n / 2 clusters. See the [DORO explorer](doro.qmd).
3. **SCAL** (Murugiah & Sweeting, 2012) fixes two count tails at every sample size, so the
   prior probability of a single cluster stays at .34 forever, while the weights are left to
   chance. Its shortcut a = b = exp(−0.033 m) collapses: at m = 100, P(K = 1) = .834. See the
   [SCAL explorer](scal.qmd).
4. **SSI** (Vicentini & Jermyn, 2025; the paper's SSI-Weight) fixes the weights and never
   mentions J, so the expected count grows without bound: 6.44 clusters at J = 25, 20.9 at
   J = 5000. See the [SSI explorer](ssi.qmd).
5. **Other defaults.** The quasi-degenerate Gamma(eps, eps) looks flat on the log scale and
   expects a single cluster; the K_n-diffuse priors of the 1990s rule out a dominant cluster;
   the Jeffreys prior piles mass on one cluster and on all singletons; the Stirling-gamma
   prior pins E(K_m) but leaves the weights unexamined. See [other defaults](other-defaults.qmd).
6. **The method map.** Placed on one plane (expected count against the majority-mass
   probability), the rules show that one alpha cannot buy few clusters and little dominance
   for free. The DPprior Dual-Anchor makes that trade explicit at the design J. See [the method map](method-map.qmd).
